mainTopic: Which items and deals fall under אונאה, the meaning of 'hand' in the פסוק, rentals, and sown seeds
overview: The amud opens with the end of the משנה. קדשים that a person must replace if lost have אונאה, and those he need not replace do not. רבי יהודה wants to add a ספר תורה, an animal, and a pearl to the list of items with no אונאה, but the חכמים refuse. The גמרא brings a ברייתא that learns each exclusion from ויקרא 25:14. 'From the hand' excludes land and slaves, 'something sold' excludes documents, and 'his brother' excludes הקדש. Along the way it teaches that even small sales of a few פרוטות have אונאה, against רב כהנא. רבה בר ממל argues that 'hand' means possession, but the גמרא uses two ברייתות to show that 'hand' normally means a real hand. אביי then rules that a rental counts as a sale for its time, so it has אונאה. Finally, רבא asks whether wheat sown in the ground still counts as loose grain or has become part of the land, and he applies that question to אונאה, oaths, and the עומר.

steps.title: Sacrifices one must replace have overcharging laws
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that קדשים a person must replace if lost have אונאה, and קדשים he need not replace do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Sacrificial animals that a person is responsible to replace have the law of overcharging. Those he is not responsible to replace do not have the law of overcharging.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes its list of exceptions to אונאה by sorting קדשים into two groups based on who bears אחריות (responsibility) for them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner must replace the animal when it is lost, it still counts as his in some way, so normal overcharging rules apply. If he has no such responsibility, the animal belongs fully to הקדש, and the earlier exclusion of הקדש covers it.

keyTerms.meaning: Overcharging or underpaying beyond the fair price in a sale
Animals set aside as offerings
Responsibility to replace something if it is lost
Obligated, responsible

steps.confusionAlert: This does not say קדשים are a new category outside הקדש. The line only sorts which consecrated animals still carry enough private ownership for אונאה to apply.

phrases.english: Sacrificial animals that he is responsible for replacing –
they have the law of overcharging.
And those he is not responsible for replacing –
they do not have the law of overcharging.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list of items excluded from אונאה, which began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קדשים with owner responsibility have אונאה. Those without it do not.

steps.title: רבי יהודה adds a Torah scroll, an animal, and a pearl
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says a ספר תורה, an animal, and a pearl also have no אונאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: Even one who sells a Torah scroll, an animal, or a pearl has no overcharging law for them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה wants to add three more items to the list of things that have no אונאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה here gives no reason, but these items have no fixed market value. A buyer may happily pay much more than usual for one he especially wants.

keyTerms.meaning: A Torah scroll
A pearl or precious gem
An animal

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Even one who sells a Torah scroll,
an animal, or a pearl –
they have no overcharging law.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אַף הַמּוֹכֵר סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a disputed extension to the list of exclusions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, a ספר תורה, an animal, and a pearl have no אונאה.

steps.title: The Sages limit the list to the items already stated
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים reply that only the items already listed are excluded from אונאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: The Sages only said these items.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים push back on רבי יהודה and refuse to add his three items.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their point is that the list of exclusions is closed. A ספר תורה, an animal, and a pearl stay under the normal אונאה rules.

keyTerms.meaning: They said to him (the other Sages' reply)
They only said…

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's exclusions from אונאה are slaves, documents, land, and הקדש, plus קדשים with no owner responsibility. The חכמים do not accept רבי יהודה's additions.

phrases.english: They said to him:
They only said these.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: לֹא אָמְרוּ אֶלָּא אֶת אֵלּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבי יהודה's addition.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רבי יהודה's extension of the list
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The list of exclusions is fixed and should not be expanded.

steps.title: The גמרא asks for the source of the exclusions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where we learn that these items have no אונאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: From where do we learn these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by asking for the Torah source of the משנה's exclusions. It is setting up the ברייתא that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question asks for a source, not a reason. The answer will come from the wording of the פסוק about אונאה.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these words learned?
The Talmud's discussion of the משנה

phrases.english: Gemara: From where are these words derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for excluding land, slaves, documents, and הקדש from אונאה.

steps.title: From hand to hand excludes land and slaves
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads 'from the hand of your fellow' as meaning movable items. That excludes land, and slaves too, since they are compared to land.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the Rabbis taught: 'And if you sell something to your fellow, or buy from the hand of your fellow' means an item acquired from hand to hand. Land is excluded, since it is not movable. Slaves are excluded, since the Torah compares them to land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא that learns the exclusions from the words of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'hand' is read literally: אונאה covers only things you can pass from one hand to another. Land can't be handed over, so it is out. עבדים are treated like land because the Torah compares them, so they are out too.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught (introduces a ברייתא)
From hand to hand
Land, real estate
Movable property
They were compared (a הקש, a Torah comparison)

phrases.english: As the Rabbis taught:
"And if you sell something to your fellow,
or buy from the hand of your fellow,"
meaning an item acquired from hand to hand.
Land is excluded, since it is not movable.
Slaves are excluded, since they are compared to land.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתָנוּ רַבָּנַן: וְכִי תִמְכְּרוּ מִמְכָּר לַעֲמִיתֶךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request for a source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'From the hand of your fellow' limits אונאה to movables, which excludes land and slaves.

steps.title: An item that is itself sold excludes documents
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא reads 'sell something sold' as meaning an item whose own substance is sold. That excludes שטרות, which matter only as proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: Documents are excluded, as it says 'And if you sell something sold,' meaning an item that is itself sold and itself bought. Documents are excluded, since they are not themselves sold or bought. They exist only for the proof written in them.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and learns the exclusion of שטרות from the doubled phrase 'sell something sold.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra word 'ממכר' teaches that the item must have value in itself. A שטר is worth something only because of the debt or right it proves, not because of the paper. So it falls outside אונאה.

keyTerms.meaning: Legal documents, such as loan contracts
Its body, the item itself
Proof or evidence

phrases.english: Documents are excluded,
as it is written: "And if you sell something sold,"
meaning something that is itself sold and itself bought.
Documents are excluded,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין גּוּפָן מָכוּר וְאֵין גּוּפָן קָנוּי,
phrases.english: since they themselves are not sold and not bought,
and they exist only for the proof in them.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָצְאוּ שְׁטָרוֹת, דִּכְתִיב: וְכִי תִמְכְּרוּ מִמְכָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא with the next exclusion.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שטרות are excluded because they have no value in themselves, only as proof.

steps.title: Documents sold to a perfumer do have overcharging
steps.stepSummary: Since the reason is that a שטר's value lies only in its proof, someone who sells old שטרות as paper to a perfumer is subject to אונאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: From here they said: One who sells his documents to a perfumer has the law of overcharging for them.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא draws a practical result from the reason it just gave for excluding שטרות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A perfumer buys the paper itself, not the proof written on it. Here the item really is 'itself sold,' so the exclusion does not apply.

keyTerms.meaning: From here they said (a ruling drawn from the reason just given)
A perfumer or spice seller

phrases.english: From here they said:
One who sells his documents to a perfumer,
phrases.notes: He sells them as plain paper, for wrapping goods, not for what's written in them.

phrases.english: has the law of overcharging for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the reason from the previous step to a related case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שטרות sold for their paper are subject to אונאה.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the perfumer ruling needed to be said at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the perfumer ruling as too obvious to need stating. It is setting up an answer that will show what the ruling really adds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling paper is like selling any other movable item, and the reason for excluding שטרות clearly doesn't apply. So why teach it?

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (a challenge that a statement adds nothing)

phrases.english: That's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the ruling in step 7.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Paper sold as paper is ordinary movable property, so of course it has אונאה.

steps.title: The ruling rejects רב כהנא: small sums have overcharging too
steps.stepSummary: The ruling was needed to reject רב כהנא, who holds there is no אונאה on sales of a few פרוטות. Old paper is that kind of cheap sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to exclude the view of רב כהנא, who says there is no overcharging for פרוטות. It teaches us that there is overcharging for פרוטות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'obvious' challenge by showing what new point the ruling makes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling isn't about whether paper counts as a real item. It is about price: even a very cheap sale, worth only small coins, is still under אונאה. That goes against רב כהנא.

keyTerms.meaning: To exclude (an opposing view)
Small coins, very small sums
It teaches us

phrases.english: It comes to exclude the view of Rav Kahana,
who says: there is no overcharging for perutot,
phrases.notes: Old paper sells for only a few small coins, so this is the kind of sale רב כהנא is talking about.

phrases.aramaic: קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן: יֵשׁ אוֹנָאָה לִפְרוּטוֹת.
phrases.english: it teaches us: there is overcharging for perutot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies the real new point of the ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without this ruling, we might think, like רב כהנא, that small-coin sales have no אונאה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even sales worth only פרוטות are subject to אונאה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the rule that a small price does not exempt a sale from אונאה.

steps.title: His brother excludes consecrated property
steps.stepSummary: הקדש is excluded because the פסוק says 'his brother,' and הקדש is not one's brother.
steps.simpleTranslation: And consecrated property? The verse says 'his brother': his brother, and not consecrated property.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the source for the last exclusion in the משנה, הקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אונאה is a law between two people. Property that belongs to the Temple is not 'your brother,' so selling it is not covered.

keyTerms.meaning: Property consecrated to the Temple
The verse says
His brother, a fellow Jew

phrases.english: Consecrated property?
The verse says "his brother" –
his brother, and not consecrated property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the list of sources after the perfumer side point.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Where do we learn that הקדש has no אונאה?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: From the word 'his brother' in the פסוק.

steps.title: Does 'his hand' always mean an actual hand?
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר ממל attacks the ברייתא's literal reading of 'hand,' using a פסוק where 'hand' clearly can't mean a physical hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר ממל challenges it: Wherever it says 'his hand,' does it mean his actual hand? If so, what about the verse 'and he took all his land from his hand'? Would you say he was holding all the land in his hand?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר ממל challenges the source for excluding land, which was built on the word 'hand.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא assumed 'from the hand' means physically passed from hand to hand. רבה בר ממל points to a פסוק about land being taken 'from his hand.' Nobody holds land in his hand, so 'hand' there can't be literal.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenges it
Actual, literal
But if so… (introduces an absurd result)

phrases.english: Rabba bar Memel challenges it:
Wherever it is written "his hand,"
is it his actual hand?
But if so,
what is written: "And he took all his land from his hand,"
would you also say that the whole land
he was holding in his hand?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to attack the derivation in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's derivation excluding land from 'מיד עמיתך'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another פסוק uses 'hand' for land, which can't be held, so 'hand' must not mean a physical hand.

steps.title: רבה בר ממל argues 'hand' means possession, undermining the proof about land
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר ממל concludes that 'hand' means possession, both in that פסוק and in the אונאה פסוק. So 'from the hand' cannot exclude land.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means from his possession. Here too, it means from his possession.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר ממל finishes his challenge: 'hand' means ownership, so the ברייתא's reason for excluding land doesn't work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land also passes from one person's possession to another's. So reading 'hand' as possession leaves no basis in this word for excluding land. Step 15 answers this challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: His possession or domain
Here too

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא learns the exclusions from ויקרא 25:14: 'from the hand' for land and slaves, 'something sold' for documents, and 'his brother' for הקדש. רבה בר ממל challenges the 'hand' derivation, arguing that 'hand' means possession.

phrases.english: Rather, it means from his possession;
here too, it means from his possession.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבה בר ממל's challenge.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to רבה בר ממל, 'hand' means possession, which would undercut the ברייתא's source for excluding land. Step 15 rejects this.

steps.title: A ברייתא about a thief shows 'hand' means a real hand
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבה בר ממל's idea that 'hand' means possession. It brings a ברייתא about a thief that needed an extra word to include his roof and courtyard. That shows 'hand' alone would have meant his real hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does 'his hand' really never mean a real hand? A ברייתא teaches: 'If the theft is surely found in his hand.' From this I only know about his hand. How do I know about his roof, courtyard, or enclosure? The doubled words 'surely found' include any place. So the only reason those places are included is the doubled wording. Without it, we would have said that 'his hand' means his actual hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבה בר ממל's conclusion from step 12. It quotes a ברייתא that treats 'his hand' as a real, physical hand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא needed a separate extra word ('הִמָּצֵא תִמָּצֵא') to include places the thief owns. That only makes sense if 'בְיָדוֹ' by itself means his physical hand. So 'hand' does not automatically mean possession.

keyTerms.meaning: his actual, physical hand
'surely be found', a doubled verb used to include more cases
his roof, his courtyard, and his enclosure (places he owns)
in any case / anywhere
I would have thought

phrases.english: And everywhere that "his hand" is written,
is it not his actual hand?
phrases.notes: This is aimed at רבה בר ממל, who just said 'hand' means possession.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught in a ברייתא:
"If [the theft] is surely found in his hand,"
I have only his hand.
His roof, his courtyard, and his enclosure, from where do we know?
The verse says: "If it is surely found,"
meaning, in any case.
The reason is that the Torah wrote "if it is surely found";
but if not for that, I would have said:

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל הֵיכָא דִּכְתַב ״יָדוֹ״, יָדוֹ מַמָּשׁ הוּא.
phrases.english: wherever "his hand" is written, it means his actual hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֹל הֵיכָא דִּכְתִיב ״יָדוֹ״, לָאו יָדוֹ מַמָּשׁ הוּא? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion of step 12 that 'hand' means possession.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר ממל's claim that 'hand' in the Torah means possession
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'hand' already meant possession, the ברייתא would not need an extra word to include the thief's roof and courtyard.

steps.title: A second ברייתא about a גט shows the same thing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds a second ברייתא, about giving a גט into a woman's hand. Again an extra word was needed to include her roof and courtyard, so 'hand' alone means a real hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: And also, a ברייתא teaches: 'And he places it in her hand.' From this I only know about her hand. How do I know about her roof, courtyard, or enclosure? The word 'and he places' includes any place. So the only reason those places are included is the word 'and he places.' Without it, we would have said that 'his hand' means an actual hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second source that backs up the same challenge. This time the case is a גט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pattern is the same as the thief case: the word 'בְּיָדָהּ' alone covers only her physical hand. A separate word, 'וְנָתַן', is needed to include her property. Two separate ברייתות now treat 'hand' as a real hand.

keyTerms.meaning: and furthermore / and also
'and he places it in her hand', said about giving a גט
'the Merciful One', meaning the Torah

phrases.english: And furthermore, it is taught in a ברייתא:
"And he places it in her hand,"
I have only her hand.
Her roof, her courtyard, and her enclosure, from where do we know?
The verse says: "And he places,"
meaning, in any case.
The reason is that the Torah wrote "and he places";
but if not for that, I would have said:
wherever "his hand" is written, it means his actual hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second source to strengthen the challenge from step 13.
steps.raayaObject: That 'hand' in the Torah normally means a physical hand
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא on 'וְנָתַן בְּיָדָהּ' about a גט

steps.title: 'Hand' means a real hand, except where that is impossible
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that 'hand' always means a real hand. The פסוק רבה בר ממל quoted is different, because a real hand makes no sense there, so it must mean possession.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, every 'his hand' means his actual hand. It is different there, in that one פסוק, because you cannot say that. There it must mean 'in his possession.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects רבה בר ממל's attack and sets the rule: 'hand' means a physical hand. The פסוק he brought is a special exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה בר ממל took one unusual פסוק and turned it into a general rule. The גמרא flips this: the normal meaning is a real hand, and only where that is impossible does it mean possession. So the ברייתא's reading of 'מִיַּד' as a real hand, which leaves out land, stands.

keyTerms.meaning: but it is different there
where it is impossible to say so
in his possession / under his control

steps.whatToRemember: In the Torah, 'his hand' means a real, physical hand. Only where that cannot work does it mean 'possession.' So the ברייתא's reading stands: land, which cannot be handed over, is left out of אונאה.
steps.confusionAlert: This conclusion reverses step 12. רבה בר ממל's reading of 'hand' as possession is NOT the final word.

phrases.english: Rather, every "his hand"
means his actual hand.
And it is different there,
phrases.notes: 'There' is the פסוק רבה בר ממל quoted about a whole land taken 'from his hand' (במדבר 21:26).

phrases.english: since it is impossible to say that,
so it means: in his possession.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the two ברייתות and limits רבה בר ממל's פסוק to an exception.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: 'His hand' means a physical hand everywhere, except where that is impossible. So the ברייתא's exclusion of land from אונאה stands.

steps.title: Does אונאה apply to renting?
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא asks whether the rules of overcharging apply to a rental. The פסוק says 'sale', so maybe only sales count, or maybe renting is no different.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא asked: Does a rental have אונאה, or does it not? The Torah said 'a sale', but not a rental. Or maybe there is no difference?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבי זירא asks whether overcharging rules apply to renting, not just to selling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The אונאה פסוק uses the word 'מִמְכָּר' (sale). The question is whether that word limits the law to real sales, or whether a rental fits inside it too.

keyTerms.meaning: he asked / raised an open question
renting / a rental
a sale, the word used in the אונאה פסוק
or perhaps there is no difference

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira asked:
Does a rental have [the law of] overcharging,
or does it not have overcharging?
The Torah said "a sale,"
but not a rental,
or perhaps there is no difference?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַבִּי זֵירָא: שְׂכִירוּת יֵשׁ לוֹ אוֹנָאָה, אוֹ אֵין לוֹ אוֹנָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question about which deals are covered by אונאה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the word 'מִמְכָּר' limits אונאה to sales, or also includes rentals

steps.title: אביי: a rental is a sale for its time
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the פסוק does not say 'a permanent sale.' It just says 'a sale', and a rental is a sale for its time period. So אונאה applies.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Is it written 'a sale forever'? It just says 'a sale.' And this, a rental, is also a sale for its day.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers רבי זירא's question. Renting counts as a sale, so אונאה applies to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah wrote 'מִמְכָּר' with no limit. Nothing says the sale has to be permanent. A rental is simply selling the use of something for a set time, so it fits inside the word 'sale.'

keyTerms.meaning: is it written?
forever / permanently
plainly, with no extra detail
for its day (its time period), it is a sale

steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, a rental is a sale for a limited time, so the rules of אונאה apply to rentals too.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
Is it written "a sale forever"?
Just "a sale" is written, with nothing added,
and this one too,
for its day, it is a sale.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: מִי כְּתִיב ״מִמְכָּר לְעוֹלָם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי זירא's question from step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: אונאה applies to rentals, because a rental is a sale for a limited time, and the פסוק says 'sale' without requiring it to be permanent.

steps.title: רבא asks about wheat sown into the ground
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks whether wheat seeds that were sown in the ground still have אונאה rules like movable goods, or count as part of the land, which has no אונאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: If wheat was sown in the ground, what is the law? Do the overcharging rules apply or not? Are the seeds treated like seeds thrown into a jug, which do have overcharging rules? Or did the person make them part of the ground?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. רבא asks whether seeds planted in the ground still count as movable goods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Movable goods have אונאה rules, but land does not. Once seeds go into the soil, they could be seen as still being seeds, like seeds sitting in a jug. Or they could be seen as part of the ground. רבא wants to know which way to see them.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked; this word introduces a real question the גמרא wants to settle
Wheat kernels
A jug or jar; here it stands for seeds still sitting as loose goods
He made them lose their own identity and become part of something else (here, the ground)
Ground or land

phrases.english: Rava asked:
Wheat, and one sowed it in the ground, what is the law?
Do they have overcharging rules,
or do they not have overcharging rules?
Are they like seeds thrown into a jug,
and so they have overcharging rules,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא בַּטְּלִינְהוּ עַל גַּב אַרְעָא?
phrases.english: or perhaps he made them part of the ground?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question about the reach of אונאה. Like step 16, it asks whether something unusual still falls under the overcharging rules.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do sown seeds keep their status as movable goods with אונאה, or do they become part of the land, which has no אונאה?

steps.title: The obvious case cannot be what רבא meant
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case רבא means. Take a worker who claimed six measures but really sowed five. That deal would be canceled anyway, by רבא's own rule about measured goods.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? Should we say he said 'I sowed six measures in it,' and witnesses came and said he sowed only five? But רבא himself said: anything sold by measure, weight, or count goes back, even if the mistake is less than the overcharging amount!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask what exact case רבא's question is about. It tests one possible case and shows it does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the amount is clearly counted (six versus five), any shortfall cancels the deal. This holds even if the gap is smaller than the usual one-sixth. So in that case the question of land versus movable goods makes no difference. רבא's question must be about some other case.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? It asks for the exact situation being discussed
If you say; it brings a suggested case that will be rejected
Witnesses
Measure, weight, count: goods whose amount can be checked exactly
It goes back; the deal is canceled

steps.confusionAlert: רבא's rule does not depend on whether the seeds count as land. Any clearly measured shortfall cancels the deal. That is exactly why this case cannot be what his question is about.

phrases.english: What is the case?
If we say that he said:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the person paid to do the sowing.

phrases.english: "I threw six into it,"
phrases.notes: Six measures of seed into the field.

phrases.english: and witnesses came and said
that he threw only five into it,
but didn't Rava say:
anything that goes by measure, by weight, or by count,
even less than the overcharging amount, it goes back!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what case the question in step 18 means, and rules out the most obvious one.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading רבא's question as being about a clearly counted shortfall (six versus five).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא himself holds that any measurable shortfall cancels the deal. So in that case it would not matter whether the seeds count as land, and his question would be pointless.

steps.title: The case is sowing 'as much as needed'
steps.stepSummary: The real case is a worker who said he sowed as much as the field needed, and it turned out he did not. Here no exact amount was promised, so the question about אונאה stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he said: 'I sowed in it as much as it needed,' and it came out that he did not sow as much as it needed. Do the overcharging rules apply or not? Are the seeds like seeds thrown into a jug, which do have overcharging rules? Or did he make them part of the ground?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the correct case for רבא's question and then asks the question again in that setting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No number was given, so this is not a clearly measured sale, and רבא's 'it goes back' rule does not apply. The only way to fix the shortfall would be the one-sixth rule of אונאה. That works only if the seeds still count as movable goods. So here the land-or-goods question really matters.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; it brings the correct case after the first one was rejected
As much as it needs; a general amount with no exact number
The matter came to light; it turned out

phrases.english: Rather, where he said:
"I threw into it as much as it needed,"
and the matter came to light
that he did not throw into it as much as it needed,

phrases.aramaic: יֵשׁ לָהֶם אוֹנָאָה אוֹ אֵין לָהֶם אוֹנָאָה?
phrases.english: do they have overcharging rules or do they not have overcharging rules?

phrases.aramaic: כְּמַאן דִּשְׁדֵי בְּכַדָּא דָּמְיָין וְיֵשׁ לָהֶם אוֹנָאָה,
phrases.english: Are they like seeds thrown into a jug, and so they have overcharging rules,
or perhaps he made them part of the ground?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem from step 19 by moving the question to a case where no exact amount was promised.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא's question was about a clearly counted shortfall, like six versus five.
steps.terutzMaskana: The question is about an unmeasured promise ('as much as needed'). There only אונאה could apply, so whether the seeds count as land matters.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that אונאה matters only where the amount was not clearly set. When the amount is exactly measured, any mistake cancels the deal on its own.

steps.title: Do we take an oath over sown seeds?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks the same land-or-goods question about oaths. Do we swear over sown seeds as we would over movable goods, or not, as with land?
steps.simpleTranslation: Do we take an oath over them, or do we not take an oath over them? Are they like seeds thrown into a jug, so we take an oath over them? Or perhaps he made them part of the ground, so we do not take an oath over them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא carries the same question over to a new area of law: court oaths.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Movable goods can lead to a court oath in a money dispute, but claims about land do not. If sown seeds count as land, no oath is taken over them. If they are still like seeds in a jug, an oath would be taken. The question stays open here.

keyTerms.meaning: They take an oath (in court, over a money claim)
Over them; here, about the sown seeds

steps.whatToRemember: רבא's whole question comes down to one point: do sown seeds stay like seeds in a jug (movable goods), or do they become part of the land? The answer would decide both אונאה and oaths.

phrases.english: Do we take an oath over them,
or do we not take an oath over them?
Are they like seeds thrown into a jug
and so we take an oath over them,
or perhaps he made them part of the ground
and so we do not take an oath over them?

steps.triggerLanguage: נִשְׁבָּעִין עֲלֵיהֶן, אוֹ אֵין נִשְׁבָּעִין עֲלֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same land-or-goods question from steps 18 and 20, now for oaths.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a court oath apply to a claim about sown seeds, or are they like land, where no oath is taken?

steps.title: Does the עומר permit sown seeds?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks whether the עומר makes sown seeds permitted to eat, or does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does the עומר permit them, or does the עומר not permit them?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks a third version of his question about planted seeds, this time about the עומר. The גמרא will first ask what case he means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: New grain (חדש) may not be eaten until the עומר is brought. רבא wants to know if seeds lying in the ground count as grain that the עומר permits. This is the same 'goods or land' question he asked about אונאה and oaths.

keyTerms.meaning: The barley offering brought on the 16th of ניסן; it permits that year's new grain
Permits them
New grain that may not be eaten until the עומר is brought

phrases.english: Does the omer permit them
phrases.notes: It is still רבא asking, about the planted seeds from the last few questions.

phrases.english: or does the omer not permit them?

steps.triggerLanguage: עוֹמֶר מַתִּירָן אוֹ אֵין עוֹמֶר מַתִּירָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same question about sown seeds, now applied to the עומר.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the עומר makes planted seeds permitted, as it does loose grain.

steps.title: A משנה already covers both cases
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that a משנה already rules on crops that took root before the עומר and crops that did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If they took root, we already learned it. If they did not take root, we already learned it! As the משנה says: if they took root before the עומר, the עומר permits them. If not, they are forbidden until the next year's עומר comes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's question, saying it seems to have no point. Either way, a משנה already gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה makes the deciding factor clear: did the plants take root before the עומר? Rooted plants are permitted by this עומר. Plants that were not rooted wait for next year's עומר. So there seems to be nothing left for רבא to ask.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the circumstances?
Took root
We already learned it in a משנה

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If they took root, we already learned it,
if they did not take root, we already learned it!
As we learned in a משנה:
If they took root before the omer,
the omer permits them,
and if not, they are forbidden
until the next omer comes!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רבא's question has any case left to ask about.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's question about the עומר and sown seeds.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה already decides both possible cases, rooted and not rooted, so the question looks pointless.

steps.title: The case: harvested and sown before the עומר, not yet rooted
steps.stepSummary: רבא means grain that was harvested and sown before the עומר. The עומר passed while the seeds were in the ground, before they took root.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the question is needed. The case is where he harvested the grain and sowed it before the עומר. The עומר came and passed while the seeds were in the ground, and they had not taken root before the עומר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by narrowing רבא's question to a case the משנה does not cover.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These kernels were already grain when the עומר came, so as loose grain the עומר would permit them. But they were also not rooted, so as part of the ground they would have to wait for next year's עומר. Whether sown seeds count as goods or as land decides which rule applies.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for a specific case
He harvested them and sowed them
Passed over them, while they were in the ground

steps.whatToRemember: רבא's three questions (אונאה, oaths, עומר) all ask one thing: are seeds in the ground still loose grain, or have they become part of the land?

phrases.english: No, it is needed,
where he reaped them and sowed them before the omer,
and the omer came
and passed over them,
and they did not take root before the omer.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא דְּחַצְדִינְהוּ וְזַרְעִינְהוּ קוֹדֶם לָעוֹמֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by finding a case the משנה does not cover.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question seemed already answered by the משנה about rooted and unrooted crops.
steps.terutzMaskana: It applies to grain already harvested before the עומר and sown, but not yet rooted. The answer depends on whether sown seeds count as grain or as ground.
